answer.text:
Both devices are NMOS. The body terminal of each is
tied to the lower terminal, i.e. to its source, so that
there is no body effect in the idealised schematic.

$$\begin{array}{lll}
M_{1}:& D=V_{DD},& G=V_{in},\qquad S=V_{out}\\
M_{2}:& D=V_{out},& G=V_{in},\qquad S=0
\end{array}\qquad 
\begin{aligned}
V_{GS1}&=V_{in}-V_{out}, & V_{DS1}&=V_{DD}-V_{out}\\
V_{GS2}&=V_{in}, & V_{DS2}&=V_{out}
\end{aligned}$$

It looks like a CMOS inverter, but the two transistors
turn on and turn off together.  Let $\beta_i=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i$
and $V_t$ be common, $\lambda=0$, and let the output be
unloaded except for a capacitance.  In dc

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}\equiv I_D\tag{1}$$

### 1.  $V_{in}<V_t$: no dc output

Both transistors are off in the square law model,
$I_D=0$, and $V_{out}$ is a high impedance node.  A charge
previously stored on the load capacitance is simply held,
and in practice leaks away, essentially through the
subthreshold current of $M_2$ to ground.  There is no
actively driven state for low input.

### 2.  $V_{in}>V_t$: $M_1$ saturated, $M_2$ in triode

For $V_{in}\le V_{DD}$

$$V_{DS1}-(V_{GS1}-V_t)=V_{DD}-V_{in}+V_t>0$$

so $M_1$, when on, is saturated.
$M_2$ cannot be saturated in steady state: saturation
would require $V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_t$, i.e. $V_{GS1}\le V_t$,
so $I_{D1}=0$.

Hence from (1)

$$ \frac{\beta_1}{2}\bigl(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_t\bigr)^2
      =\beta_2\Bigl[(V_{in}-V_t)V_{out}-\frac{V_{out}^{2}}{2}\Bigr]
      \qquad V_{in}>V_t \tag{2}$$

Put $u=V_{in}-V_t$, $v=V_{out}$.  (2) is
$\beta_1(u-v)^2=\beta_2\bigl[u^{2}-(u-v)^2\bigr]$, whence

$$\,u-v=u\sqrt{\frac{\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2}}\,$$

$$\;V_{out}= 
\Biggl[1-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2}}\;\Biggr]
\bigl(V_{in}-V_t\bigr)\equiv c\,(V_{in}-V_t),\qquad 
0<c<1\; \tag{3}$$

i.e. the (ideal) transfer characteristic for $V_{in}>V_t$
is a straight line of slope $c<1$ starting at $(V_t,0)$.
$M_1$ is a source follower and $M_2$, in the triode region,
is a gate controlled non-linear resistor to ground; the
output is the ratioed division between them.  In small
signal form, $\lambda$ included,

$$ \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
\frac{g_{m1}-g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}},\qquad
R_{out}\approx\frac1{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} ,$$
which reduces to $c$ for $\lambda=0$.

For identical transistors $c=1-1/\sqrt2\approx0.29$.
E.g. $V_{DD}=V_{in}=5\,{\rm V}$, $V_t=1\,{\rm V}$ gives
$V_{out}\approx1.2\,{\rm V}$, neither a good ``1'' nor
a good ``0''.  In general the largest attainable output,
at $V_{in}=V_{DD}$, is only

$$V_{out,max}=c\,(V_{DD}-V_t)<V_{DD}-V_t .$$

Making $\beta_2\gg\beta_1$ makes $c$ small, $V_{out}$ lower
for high $V_{in}$, at the expense of ratioed operation;
making $\beta_1\gg\beta_2$ makes $c\to1$, $V_{out}\approx
V_{in}-V_t$, a poor source follower.

Whenever $V_{in}>V_t$ a dc current flows from $V_{DD}$
to ground,

$$I_D=\frac{\beta_1}{2}\bigl(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_t\bigr)^2
     =\frac{\beta_1}{2}(V_{in}-V_t)^2\,
       \frac{\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2},\qquad 
P_{stat}=V_{DD}I_D\neq0,$$

even with no load.  Transitorily, if $V_{out}$ starts
above the value (3), $M_1$ is off and $M_2$ discharges
$C_L$ until (3) is reached; if it starts below, $M_1$
charges $C_L$ up to (3).

### Conclusion

The circuit is not an inverter at all.  It is
non-inverting, with voltage gain $c<1$, no rail-to-rail
swing, a floating output for $V_{in}<V_t$, a level that
depends on $\beta_1/\beta_2$, and static power
dissipation for $V_{in}>V_t$.  It is merely an NMOS
source follower $M_1$ loaded by a triode NMOS $M_2$
whose gate is tied, unfortunately, to the same input.

The network is the basic CMOS (complementary-MOS) inverter.

1. Which device is which  
   • M1, the transistor tied to VDD, must be a p–channel MOSFET.  
     – Source at VDD, drain at the output node.  
   • M2, the transistor tied to ground, is an n-channel MOSFET.  
     – Drain at the output node, source at ground.  
   (If the upper device were n-channel its body diode would conduct whenever
   VDD > ground, so the circuit could not work.)

2. Logic (static) operation  
   a) Vin ≈ 0 V (logic 0)  
      – M1 : VSG = VDD > |VTP|  → ON  
      – M2 : VGS = 0            → OFF  
      → Output node pulled to VDD → VOH ≈ VDD (logic 1).  
      – No steady dc current because only the p-device conducts.

   b) Vin ≈ VDD (logic 1)  
      – M1 : VSG = 0            → OFF  
      – M2 : VGS = VDD > VTN    → ON  
      → Output node pulled to 0 V → VOL ≈ 0 (logic 0).  
      – Again no dc current; only the n-device conducts.

   c) Vin in the middle (around the switching point VM)  
      – Both devices partially ON; for a brief time there is a
        current path VDD → M1 → M2 → ground (the “shoot-through” or
        “crowbar” current).  This happens only while the input is
        switching, so the static power of the gate is essentially zero.

   Hence the gate produces the logical NOT of its input with rail-to-rail
   swing and almost zero static power-dissipation, which is why it is the
   work-horse of modern digital ICs.

3. Transfer characteristic and trip point VM  
   Using the long-channel square-law model in saturation and equating the
   drain currents of the two devices at the transition point:

        βn (VM – VTN)^2 = βp (VDD – VM – |VTP|)^2
        β ≜ μ Cox (W/L)

   Solving,

        VM = (βp (VDD + |VTP|) + βn VTN) / (βn + βp)

   • If |VTP| = VTN and the devices are sized so that βn = βp,
     VM = VDD / 2 (symmetrical inverter).

4. Noise margins (ideal abrupt transition)  

        NML ≈ VM – VOL       (≈ VM, because VOL ≈ 0)
        NMH ≈ VOH – VM       (≈ VDD – VM)

   For the symmetric case, NML ≈ NMH ≈ VDD/2 – VT, giving large
   tolerance to noise on both logic levels.

5. Dynamic behaviour with a load capacitance CL  

        tPHL ≈ (CL VDD) / (βn (VDD – VTN))   (high-to-low delay)  
        tPLH ≈ (CL VDD) / (βp (VDD – |VTP|)) (low-to-high delay)

   Delays are adjusted in practice by the W/L ratio (i.e. β) of the two
   transistors; typically the p-device is made wider to compensate for its
   lower mobility (µp ≈ 0.4 µn).

6. Power dissipation  

        Pstatic   ≈ 0                       (only leakage paths)  
        Pdynamic  = CL VDD² fSW             (plus the brief shoot-through
                                             component while Vin ≈ VM)

Summary  
The circuit is a complementary push-pull stage that inverts the input,
switches all the way between 0 V and VDD, exhibits large noise margins,
draws essentially no dc power, and forms the fundamental building block
for all CMOS digital logic.

The drawing is nothing more than the basic CMOS inverter.

•  M1 is a p-channel MOSFET whose drain is tied to VDD and whose source is the output node.  
•  M2 is an n-channel MOSFET whose source is tied to ground and whose drain is the same output node.  
•  The two gates are shorted together and driven by Vin.

1. Qualitative operation (logic level description)

   Vin = 0 (LOW)  
  Vgp = 0 − VDD = –VDD < Vthp ⟶ M1 ON  
  Vgn = 0           ⟶ M2 OFF  
  Output is pulled up to VDD  →  logic “1”

   Vin = VDD (HIGH)  
  Vgp = VDD − VDD = 0     ⟶ M1 OFF  
  Vgn = VDD > Vthn      ⟶ M2 ON  
  Output is pulled down to 0 V  →  logic “0”

   For Vin in the transition region both devices conduct simultaneously; a short-lived “crowbar” current flows from VDD to ground, giving the inverter its characteristic steep transfer curve.

2. DC transfer characteristic

   Treat both transistors as long-channel devices and assume they enter saturation around the switching point.  
   Idn = (βn/2)(Vin − Vthn)^2  
   Idp = (βp/2)(VDD − Vin − |Vthp|)^2  

   The switching threshold V­M is found from Idn = Idp :

        Vin − Vthn
   ----------------------  =  √(βp/βn)
    VDD − Vin − |Vthp|

   If βn ≈ βp and |Vthp| ≈ Vthn, VM ≈ VDD/2, which gives the inverter its large, almost symmetric noise margins.

3. Static power

   •  In either logic state one transistor is OFF, so the DC current is essentially zero (ideal CMOS draws no static power).  
   •  Only during switching do both devices conduct simultaneously, producing a short dynamic current spike.

4. Logic truth table

        Vin   Vout
        0  →  1
        1  →  0

   Hence the circuit implements the NOT function.

5. Key properties

   •  Rail-to-rail output swing (0 V and VDD).  
   •  Large noise margins ≈ ⅔ VDD (for symmetrical devices).  
   •  Very low static power dissipation.  
   •  High input impedance.

In summary, the two-transistor stack with a common gate connection is the fundamental CMOS inverter: it produces the logical complement of the input while dissipating power only during switching.

The two transistors form the elementary CMOS inverter (NOT gate).

1. Circuit topology  
   • M1: p-channel MOSFET (source tied to VDD).  
   • M2: n-channel MOSFET (source tied to ground).  
   • Drains of M1 and M2 are shorted; that node is Vout.  
   • Gates are shorted and driven by Vin.

2. Static (DC) operation  
   a) Vin ≈ 0 V  
      – NMOS: VGS = 0  ⇒ OFF  
      – PMOS: VSG = VDD > |VTp| ⇒ ON  
      – Vout is pulled up to VDD (logic ‘1’).  
      – No DC path from VDD to GND → zero static current.  

   b) Vin ≈ VDD  
      – NMOS: VGS = VDD > VTn ⇒ ON  
      – PMOS: VSG = 0  ⇒ OFF  
      – Vout is pulled to ground (logic ‘0’).  
      – Again no DC through-current.

   Result: the gate inverts the input, giving rail-to-rail logic levels  
        VOH ≈ VDD ,  VOL ≈ 0.

3. Switching point (VM)  
   Around the mid-range both devices conduct simultaneously.  
   Assuming both are in saturation and equating their drain currents

        IDn = βn/2 (Vin – VTn)²  
        IDp = βp/2 (VDD – Vin – |VTp|)²

        βn(Vin – VTn)² = βp(VDD – Vin – |VTp|)²

        VM = [VTn + k(VDD – |VTp|)] / (1 + k) ,
        k = √(βp/βn)  ,  β = μCox(W/L).

   Choosing W/L so that k ≈ 1 places VM near VDD/2 and yields large, nearly symmetrical noise
   margins
        NMH ≈ VDD – VM ,  NML ≈ VM.

4. Dynamic behaviour  
   • Only a short-lived current flows from VDD to GND while Vin crosses VM, so static power is
     essentially zero.  
   • With a load capacitance C_L,

        tpHL ≈ Rn C_L ,  tpLH ≈ Rp C_L ,
        tp ≈ (tpHL + tpLH)/2.

     Rn and Rp are the on-resistances evaluated at the appropriate overdrive voltages.  
   • Average dynamic power: Pdyn = α C_L VDD² f (α = switching activity factor).

5. Key advantages  
   – Full-swing outputs (0 → VDD).  
   – Large noise margins.  
   – Very low quiescent power.  
   – Basis of all static CMOS logic.

Hence the figure is the canonical CMOS inverter, and its behaviour is completely described by the transfer point VM derived above, the rail-to-rail output levels, the large noise margins, and the very low static power dissipation.

The circuit shown is a simple CMOS inverter, also known as an inverting buffer or NOT gate. It consists of two transistors: \( M_1 \) and \( M_2 \).

### Components:
- \( M_1 \): A p-channel MOSFET (PMOS)
- \( M_2 \): An n-channel MOSFET (NMOS)
- \( V_{DD} \): The positive power supply voltage
- \( V_{in} \): The input voltage
- \( V_{out} \): The output voltage

### Operation:

#### 1. When \( V_{in} \) is Low (0V or near ground):
- \( M_1 \) (PMOS) is ON because its gate-to-source voltage (\( V_{GS} \)) is negative, which turns it on.
- \( M_2 \) (NMOS) is OFF because its gate-to-source voltage (\( V_{GS} \)) is zero or positive but not enough to turn it on.

Since \( M_1 \) is ON, it connects \( V_{out} \) to \( V_{DD} \), making \( V_{out} \) high (approximately \( V_{DD} \)).

#### 2. When \( V_{in} \) is High (\( V_{DD} \)):
- \( M_1 \) (PMOS) is OFF because its gate-to-source voltage (\( V_{GS} \)) is zero or positive, which turns it off.
- \( M_2 \) (NMOS) is ON because its gate-to-source voltage (\( V_{GS} \)) is positive, which turns it on.

Since \( M_2 \) is ON, it connects \( V_{out} \) to ground, making \( V_{out} \) low (approximately 0V).

### Summary:
- The CMOS inverter inverts the input signal. If the input is high, the output is low, and if the input is low, the output is high.
- This circuit has very low static power consumption because only one transistor is on at any given time.
- The output impedance is low when either transistor is on, providing good drive capability for subsequent stages.

This is exactly the *topology* of a CMOS inverter. The decisive detail, however, is the **device type**: the two symbols are drawn **identically** (same arrow direction, no inversion bubble at either gate). A true inverter requires the upper device to be a **PMOS** and the lower an **NMOS**. As drawn, M1 and M2 are the **same type**, and that single fact changes the whole behaviour. I analyse both interpretations below.

## 2. As drawn – identical devices (the "trick")

### Case A: both NMOS
Let $V_{th}>0$.

* **M2** (S = GND): on when $V_{GS}=V_{in}>V_{th}$.
* **M1** (S = $V_{DD}$, the higher‑potential terminal): on only when $V_{GS}=V_{in}-V_{DD}>V_{th}$, i.e. $V_{in}>V_{DD}+V_{th}$ — **impossible** for $0\le V_{in}\le V_{DD}$. So **M1 is always OFF**; it can never pull $V_{out}$ up.

KCL at $V_{out}$ then forces:

* $V_{in}>V_{th}$: M2 would source current unless $V_{DS}=0$, so $V_{out}\to 0$.
* $V_{in}\le V_{th}$: both devices off → the $V_{out}$ node has **no DC path** → $V_{out}$ is **floating** (set by initial charge/parasitics).

So the "high" level is never established. The VTC is $V_{out}=0$ for $V_{in}>V_{th}$ and **undefined** for $V_{in}\le V_{th}$.

### Case B: both PMOS
Let $|V_{th}|>0$.

* **M1** (S = $V_{DD}$): on when $V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_{th}|$.
* **M2** (S = $V_{out}$): on when $V_{out}-V_{in}>|V_{th}|$.

At $V_{in}=0$, both conduct; equating the currents (M1 in triode, M2 in saturation) with $a=V_{DD}-|V_{th}|$, $b=V_{out}-|V_{th}|$ gives $a^2=2b^2$, i.e.
$$V_{out}\big|_{V_{in}=0} = |V_{th}|+\frac{V_{DD}-|V_{th}|}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.7\,V_{DD}$$
At $V_{in}=V_{DD}$, M1 is off and M2 is also off ($V_{SG}=V_{out}-V_{DD}\le0$) → **$V_{out}$ floats** again.

So the "high" is only ≈0.7 $V_{DD}$ (not rail‑to‑rail) and the "low" floats.

**Conclusion for the as‑drawn circuit:** with like‑type devices there is always an input region where **both transistors are off**, leaving $V_{out}$ floating, and the opposite rail is not pulled to its full value. The circuit therefore **does not function as a valid digital inverter** (no defined output for one logic level, degraded noise margins).

## 3. If the intention was a proper CMOS inverter (M1 = PMOS, M2 = NMOS)

Then the device types are opposite and the floating regions disappear:

* $V_{in}=0$ → PMOS on ($V_{SG}=V_{DD}$), NMOS off → $V_{out}=V_{DD}$ (full high; the PMOS passes a strong '1').
* $V_{in}=V_{DD}$ → NMOS on ($V_{GS}=V_{DD}$), PMOS off → $V_{out}=0$ (full low; the NMOS passes a strong '0').

This gives rail‑to‑rail output, a steep VTC, and large noise margins — the intended inverter behaviour.

| Interpretation | $V_{out}$ for $V_{in}=0$ | $V_{out}$ for $V_{in}=V_{DD}$ | Inverter? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Both NMOS (as drawn) | **floating** | 0 | No |

## Circuit identification

The schematic is the standard **CMOS inverter** (the basic building block of digital logic). Two enhancement‑mode MOSFETs are stacked between the supplies, their gates are tied together to the input $V_{in}$, and their common drain node is the output $V_{out}$:

* **$M_1$ (top) = PMOS** – the *pull‑up* device. Its source is the $V_{DD}$ node, its drain is $V_{out}$.
* **$M_2$ (bottom) = NMOS** – the *pull‑down* device. Its source is the ground node, its drain is $V_{out}$.
* The arrow on each symbol marks the source terminal, which is why the source of $M_1$ sits at the positive rail and the source of $M_2$ sits at ground.

The two devices have **complementary** gate control: a low $V_{in}$ turns on the PMOS, a high $V_{in}$ turns on the NMOS.

## Static (DC) operation

| $V_{in}$ | $M_1$ (PMOS) | $M_2$ (NMOS) | $V_{out}$ | Logic |
|---------|--------------|--------------|-----------|-------|
| Low ($0$) | ON (resistor to $V_{DD}$) | OFF | $\approx V_{DD}$ | **1** |
| High ($V_{DD}$) | OFF | ON (resistor to GND) | $\approx 0$ | **0** |

* **$V_{in}=0$:** $V_{GS2}=0<V_{thn}$ so $M_2$ is cut off. $V_{SG1}=V_{DD}>|V_{thp}|$ so $M_1$ conducts; with $V_{out}\to V_{DD}$, $V_{SD1}$ is small and $M_1$ operates in the **triode** region, acting as a low‑resistance path to $V_{DD}$. With no DC load current, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.
* **$V_{in}=V_{DD}$:** $V_{GS1}=0<|V_{thp}|$ so $M_1$ is cut off. $V_{GS2}=V_{DD}>V_{thn}$ so $M_2$ conducts; $V_{out}\to 0$ puts $M_2$ in **triode**, a low‑resistance path to ground. With no load current, $V_{out}=0$.

Because in every steady state **one transistor is always off**, there is no DC path from $V_{DD}$ to ground:

$$P_{static} = 0$$

This zero static power dissipation (only leakage flows) is the defining advantage of CMOS over resistor‑pull‑up or NMOS logic.

## Transition region and the $V_I$ characteristic

As $V_{in}$ sweeps from $0$ to $V_{DD}$, $V_{out}$ sweeps from $V_{DD}$ to $0$:

1. **$0 \le V_{in} < V_{thn}$:** $M_2$ off, $M_1$ in triode → $V_{out}\approx V_{DD}$ (flat top).
2. **$V_{thn} < V_{in} < V_{DD}-|V_{thp}|$:** both devices conduct. Initially both are in saturation, giving the steepest slope of the $V_I$ curve; as $V_{out}$ falls, $M_1$ leaves saturation first (enters triode) while $M_2$ stays in saturation, then $M_2$ also enters triode.
3. **$V_{in} > V_{DD}-|V_{thp}|$:** $M_1$ off, $M_2$ in triode → $V_{out}\approx 0$ (flat bottom).

The slope in the middle is made very large (nearly vertical) by high device transconductances, so the inverter behaves as a sharp inverting switch.

**Switching threshold $V_M$** (the point where $V_{out}=V_{in}$) is set by the relative strengths of the two devices:

$$V_M = \frac{V_{DD}+V_{thn}-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_n}{\beta_p}\,(V_{DD}-V_{thn}-V_{thp})^2}}{1+\sqrt{\beta_n/\beta_p}},\quad \beta_i = k_i' \frac{W_i}{L_i}$$

For equal strengths ($\beta_n=\beta_p$) and matched thresholds, $V_M \approx V_{DD}/2$, which is desirable.

## Noise margins

With the $V_I$ curve characterized by $V_{IL},\,V_{OH},\,V_{OL},\,V_{HH}$, the inverter provides two noise margins:

$$NM_L = V_{IL}-V_{OL}\approx V_{IL},\qquad NM_H = V_{OH}-V_{HH}=V_{DD}-V_{DD}=V_{DD}-V_{HH}$$

These margins are large when the transition is steep, i.e. when the devices are sized generously.

## Dynamic power

Although static power is zero, switching the output load capacitance $C_L$ and the short‑circuit current during the transition dissipate energy:

$$P_{dyn} = \underbrace{C_L V_{DD}^2 f}_{\text{charging/discharging } C_L} + \underbrace{P_{sc}}_{\text{short‑circuit (both on)}}$$

The short‑circuit term is minimized by making the transition (and the overlap of conduction) as fast as possible.

## Design notes

* **Sizing ratio $W_{M1}/W_{M2}$** is chosen to (a) place $V_M$ near $V_{DD}/2$ and (b) balance rise and fall times. Because $\mu_n \approx 2\,\mu_p$, the PMOS is typically made wider (larger $W/L$) than the NMOS for symmetric drive.
* **Minimum device lengths** set the speed and the steepness of the $V_I$ curve.
* The inverter inverts logic, has rail‑to‑rail output swing, zero DC power, and high noise immunity — which is why it is the universal cell of CMOS digital circuits.

**Summary:** the figure is a CMOS inverter — a PMOS pull‑up ($M_1$) and an NMOS pull‑down ($M_2$) with common gate $V_{in}$ and common drain $V_{out}$. It produces $V_{out}=\overline{V_{in}}$, draws no static power, and its sharp $V_I$ transition, threshold $V_M\approx V_{DD}/2$, and noise margins are governed by the relative $W/L$ of the two transistors.

**Input low, $V_{in}=0$:**
* M2 (NMOS): $V_{GS2}=0 < V_{thn}$ → **OFF** (open switch to ground).

**Input high, $V_{in}=V_{DD}$:**
* M1 (PMOS): $V_{SG1}=0 < |V_{thp}|$ → **OFF** (open switch to $V_{DD}$).
* M2 (NMOS): $V_{GS2}=V_{DD} > V_{thn}$ → **ON**. As $V_{out}$ falls toward 0, M2 is in its linear region and pulls the node to ground.
* Result: $V_{out}=0$ (logic 0). Again **quiescent power = 0**.

**Transition region, $V_{thn}<V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_{thp}|$:**
Both transistors conduct. The node $V_{out}$ is determined by the ratio of the two currents and falls steeply from $V_{DD}$ to 0 as $V_{in}$ rises — this is where the device acts as a high‑gain **inverting amplifier** (the slope $dV_{out}/dV_{in}$ is large and negative).

$$\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mu_n C_{ox}\!\left(\tfrac{W}{L}\right)_n (V_M - V_{thn})^2 \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mu_p C_{ox}\!\left(\tfrac{W}{L}\right)_p (V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{thp}|)^2$$

## Dynamic (short‑circuit) current

While $V_{in}$ is ramping, there is a brief interval in which **both** M1 and M2 are on, creating a direct $V_{DD}\rightarrow$ GND path. This produces a transient "crowbar" current $I_{sc}$, which is the dominant source of dynamic power in CMOS. The smaller the transition time, the larger $I_{sc}$.

## Summary of the VTC

| $V_{in}$ range | M1 (PMOS) | M2 (NMOS) | $V_{out}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $< V_{thn}$ | ON | OFF | $V_{DD}$ |
| $V_{thn}\dots V_{DD}-|V_{thp}|$ | ON | ON | falls steeply (gain region) |
| $> V_{DD}-|V_{thp}|$ | OFF | ON | 0 |

Hence the circuit is a **rail‑to‑rail, zero‑static‑power, inverting CMOS gate** with a steep, high‑gain transition centered near $V_M$.

---

**Remark on the device symbols.** The supply connections (top to $V_{DD}$, bottom to GND) *require* M1 to be PMOS and M2 NMOS for the inverter action above. If, instead, both transistors were the same type (as the identical arrow directions in the drawing might suggest), the circuit would **not** be a functional inverter: with $V_{in}=0$ both devices would be off and $V_{out}$ would be left floating (high‑impedance), and with $V_{in}$ high the two like‑type devices would merely settle at an intermediate voltage.     *   The **Source** of the NMOS ($M_2$) is connected to Ground.

**4. Operation / Logic Function**
The circuit operates based on the complementary switching of the two transistors:

*   **When Input is Low ($V_{in} \approx 0\text{V}$):**

    *   **$M_2$ (NMOS):** The gate-source voltage $V_{GS} = V_{in} - 0\text{V}$ is near 0V (below threshold). Thus, $M_2$ is **OFF** (non-conducting).
    *   **Result:** Current flows from $V_{DD}$ through $M_1$ to the output. The output $V_{out}$ is pulled high to approximately $V_{DD}$ (Logic High / 1).

*   **When Input is High ($V_{in} \approx V_{DD}$):**
    *   **$M_1$ (PMOS):** The gate-source voltage $V_{GS} \approx 0\text{V}$. Thus, $M_1$ is **OFF**.

    *   **Result:** Current flows from the output through $M_2$ to Ground. The output $V_{out}$ is pulled low to approximately 0V (Logic Low / 0).

This circuit is a basic **NOT gate**. It inverts the input signal:
*   Input 0 $\rightarrow$ Output 1
*   Input 1 $\rightarrow$ Output 0
